_comment: Seed content for the Object of the Day pack. Same shape as trees.json and read by the same seed script and the same engine — no pack-specific code anywhere. Lives outside src/ because it holds answers. Hints are ordered easy -> hard and never contain the answer or a closeTerm.

hints: A tiny piece of bent wire that has barely changed in over a century.
It holds a few sheets together without piercing them.
The standard shape is a double oval, known as the Gem pattern.
Norwegians wore one on the lapel as a quiet symbol of resistance during the occupation.
Its most famous digital incarnation was an animated assistant in Microsoft Office.
puzzles.fact: The double-oval Gem design was never patented by the man usually credited with it. Norwegians wore one on the lapel during the Nazi occupation as a silent sign of unity.

hints: A portable canopy on a folding frame, carried in one hand.
Ribs radiate from a central shaft and lock open with a spring catch.
It was a sunshade for millennia before anyone thought to waterproof one.
Superstition says opening one indoors invites bad luck.
Jonas Hanway was mocked in the streets for carrying one through 1750s London.
puzzles.fact: It existed as a sunshade in ancient Egypt and China for thousands of years before waterproofed versions appeared. Jonas Hanway was ridiculed for carrying one in 1750s London.

hints: A spring-loaded desk tool that joins sheets with a small metal fastener.
Press down and a thin wire clip is driven through the paper and bent flat underneath.
The plate in the base swivels, so the wire can be bent outward instead.
An early ornate model was supposedly made for King Louis XV, one sheet at a time.
A red Swingline model became the emotional centre of the film Office Space.
puzzles.fact: The anvil in the base rotates: one setting clinches the wire inward for permanent binding, the other bends it outward so the sheets can be pulled apart again cleanly.

hints: A helix of steel with a handle, kept in almost every kitchen drawer.
It descended from a tool for pulling wadding out of musket barrels.
The winged variety uses two levers that rise as you turn the centre.
Sommeliers prefer the folding pocket version with a small blade and a hinged fulcrum.
Its entire job is to defeat a compressed plug of oak bark.
puzzles.fact: It evolved from the bulletscrew, a worm on a rod used to pull wadding and stuck shot out of musket barrels — which is why the business end is still called the worm.

hints: Two rows of interlocking teeth joined by a sliding tab.
It replaced long rows of buttons and hooks on boots and trousers.
The tab's Y-shaped channel does all the work, meshing or parting the teeth.
B. F. Goodrich is credited with naming it after the sound it makes.
Aldous Huxley made it a symbol of frictionless modernity in Brave New World.
puzzles.fact: The slider is just a Y-shaped channel: pulled one way it forces the teeth to mesh, pulled the other it wedges them apart. Nothing inside it moves at all.

hints: A bundle of thin wire loops fixed into a handle.
Its purpose is to force air into something until the texture changes.
The balloon shape suits egg whites; a flat coil suits sauces in a pan.
Before wire, cooks bundled birch twigs together for the same job.
It is what turns liquid cream into something that holds a peak.
puzzles.fact: It works by dragging air into the liquid and shearing proteins so they unfold and trap the bubbles. A bundle of birch twigs did the same job for centuries.

hints: A portable, detachable security device with a hinged metal loop.
The U-shaped shackle springs free when the right key is turned.
Inside, a stack of spring-loaded pin pairs must align along a shear line.
Couples attach them to bridge railings until the weight becomes a hazard.
Versions without a keyway use a rotating numbered dial instead.
puzzles.fact: The pin-tumbler mechanism inside is essentially unchanged from ancient Egyptian designs: a row of pins of differing lengths that only line up along the shear line for the right key.

hints: A countertop box with slots, found in most kitchens.
Nichrome wire glows orange behind a sheet of mica to do the work.
A bimetallic strip bends as it warms, which is how it knows when to stop.
The spring-loaded carriage releases and jumps up when the circuit opens.
Its output is browned bread, thanks to the Maillard reaction.
puzzles.fact: The timer is not a clock — a bimetallic strip warms and bends until it releases the catch, which is why the same setting browns differently on a cold morning.

hints: Two glass bulbs joined at a narrow waist, usually held in a wooden frame.
It measures one fixed interval and nothing else — it cannot tell you what time it is.
The flow rate depends on the aperture, not on how much is still waiting above.
Ships used them alongside a knotted line to work out their speed.
Turn it over and it starts again; carved on tombstones it means time is running out.
puzzles.fact: Unlike water, granular flow through the neck stays constant regardless of how much is left above it — which is why it keeps time accurately from start to finish.

hints: A single-wheeled carrier with two handles, on every building site.
It is a second-class lever: the load sits between the pivot and your hands.
That geometry means you lift only part of the weight; the ground takes the rest.
Han dynasty China had them centuries before Europe did.
Tip it forward and the whole load slides out exactly where you want it.
puzzles.fact: Because it is a second-class lever, the person lifting carries only a fraction of the load — the rest is borne by the wheel, which is why one person can move what two could not carry.

hints: A single length of sprung wire bent back on itself, with a clasp at one end.
The coil at the base provides the tension that keeps the sharp end seated.
A small sheath covers the point so it cannot prick the wearer.
Walter Hunt devised it in 1849, reportedly to settle a fifteen-dollar debt.
Punk fashion adopted it as jewellery and as a badge of do-it-yourself defiance.
puzzles.fact: Walter Hunt patented it in 1849 and sold the rights for $400 to clear a $15 debt. The buyer made a fortune from it.

hints: A double-walled container that keeps its contents at whatever temperature you gave them.
The gap between the walls is evacuated, so conduction and convection have nothing to cross.
A silvered mirror finish on the inner surface reflects radiant heat back where it came from.
James Dewar built the first one to hold liquefied gases in his laboratory.
An old joke asks how it knows whether to keep things hot or cold.
puzzles.fact: James Dewar built it in 1892 to store liquefied gases and never patented it. A German glassblower commercialised the idea under a brand name that became the everyday word for it.

hints: A perforated bowl that appears in the sink at the end of cooking pasta.
Its holes are wide enough to pass water instantly while holding back the solids.
Usually stainless steel or plastic, standing on a foot ring or two side handles.
Members of one parody religion have gone to court for the right to wear one in ID photos.
The finer mesh-lined version of the same idea is a different tool with a different name.
puzzles.fact: Pastafarians have won the right in several jurisdictions to wear one in official identity photographs, on the grounds that it counts as religious headgear.

hints: The default writing instrument of the twentieth century, given away by the million.
A tiny rotating sphere set in a socket meters thick ink onto the page.
Its oil-based ink dries almost on contact, unlike the water-based stuff before it.
Its Hungarian-Argentine inventor got the idea watching how fast newspaper ink dried.
The hole in the barrel is a safety measure, so a swallowed cap cannot seal the airway.
puzzles.fact: The small hole in the barrel of the cheapest models exists so that a cap lodged in someone's throat still lets air through — a design change made after several choking deaths.

hints: A palm-sized instrument that always answers the same single question.
A magnetised needle floats in liquid, which damps its swing.
It points at a wandering magnetic spot, not the geographic one — the gap is called declination.
Chinese diviners used lodestone versions long before any sailor did.
A rotating bezel lets you set a bearing and walk it across open ground.
puzzles.fact: It points at the magnetic pole, which drifts — currently at tens of kilometres a year — so charts must state the local declination and the year it was measured.

hints: A pyramid-shaped box that sits on a piano and is widely resented.
An inverted pendulum with a sliding weight sets the rate.
Move the weight upward and it ticks more slowly, which surprises most people.
Its markings run from grave through andante to prestissimo.
Maelzel patented it, and Beethoven was among the first to mark scores with its numbers.
puzzles.fact: It is an inverted pendulum, so sliding the weight up slows it down — the opposite of a clock pendulum. Beethoven was among the first composers to publish tempo markings using it.

hints: A straight bar with a small sealed glass tube set into its face.
The tube holds liquid, but is deliberately not filled all the way.
The trapped bubble rises to the highest point, and that is what you read.
Alcohol is used rather than water: it stays fluid in the cold and moves freely.
Extra tubes set at right angles let you check plumb as well as horizontal.
puzzles.fact: The tube is very slightly curved, so the bubble sits at its highest point. Alcohol is used because it has low viscosity and will not freeze on a winter site.

hints: A mechanical machine that puts one character on paper per keystroke.
Each key swings a hammer against an inked ribbon.
A bell warns that the line is nearly full, and a lever returns the carriage.
Its key arrangement was designed partly to stop adjacent hammers colliding.
That layout, QWERTY, has outlived the machine by many decades.
puzzles.fact: QWERTY was arranged partly to separate letters commonly typed in sequence, so the hammers were less likely to jam. The layout survived the mechanism that required it.

hints: A wooden frame of rods with beads that slide along them.
Each rod is a place value, and the beads are the digits.
On the classic design the upper beads are worth five and the lower ones one.
A skilled user beat an electric calculator in a famous 1946 contest in Tokyo.
Practised operators eventually stop touching it and picture the beads instead.
puzzles.fact: In a 1946 Tokyo contest a Japanese clerk beat a US Army electric calculator at addition, subtraction and division. Expert users can compute mentally by visualising the beads.

hints: A flat wooden base with a violently spring-loaded steel bar.
A bait pedal releases the catch, and the bar swings over in a hundredth of a second.
The classic Little Nipper design dates from 1899 and has barely changed since.
It gave rise to a proverb about invention and a beaten path to your door.
Physicists filmed rooms full of them loaded with ping-pong balls to demonstrate chain reactions.
puzzles.fact: It is among the most-patented devices in history — the US patent office has granted over 4,400 for the category — yet the 1899 sprung-bar design still outsells everything since.

hints: A coiled metal ribbon in a palm-sized case, clipped to a builder's belt.
The ribbon is curved across its width, which is what keeps it rigid when extended.
A spring recoils it, and a thumb catch holds it wherever you stop.
The hooked end slides by exactly its own thickness, which is not a fault.
That deliberate play makes the reading identical whether you push against something or pull from it.
puzzles.fact: The loose hook is intentional: it slides by exactly the thickness of the metal, so an inside measurement and an outside measurement both read true from the same zero.

hints: A hand-worked cylinder with a plunger and a flexible hose.
A one-way valve admits air on the up-stroke and refuses to give it back on the down.
The barrel gets noticeably warm, because compressing a gas heats it.
The larger kind stands on the floor with a gauge and a plate for your foot.
The head has to match either a Presta or a Schrader fitting.
puzzles.fact: The barrel warms because compressing a gas raises its temperature — the same physics as a diesel engine's ignition, just at a far smaller scale.

hints: A red pressurised cylinder bracketed to the wall of nearly every public building.
A pin has to be pulled before the lever will do anything at all.
Its label carries a colour band saying which classes of blaze it suits.
The carbon dioxide type has a wide horn that gets cold enough to burn skin.
The drill is remembered as PASS: pull, aim, squeeze, sweep.
puzzles.fact: Using the wrong class makes things worse — water on a chip-pan blaze flashes to steam and throws burning oil across the room, which is why the colour bands exist.

hints: A garden ornament that is also an instrument, and needs no power at all.
A raised blade called a gnomon casts the shadow you read.
Double-checking against a clock is confusing: it runs ahead in some months and behind in others.
The blade has to be tilted to match your latitude or the readings drift all year.
Mottoes carved on the face traditionally remind you that the hours are slipping away.
puzzles.fact: It keeps solar time, which drifts up to about 16 minutes ahead of or behind clock time across the year — a discrepancy called the equation of time.

hints: Two strips that grip each other and part with a distinctive tearing sound.
One face is stiff hooks; the other is a dense field of soft loops.
It came from a walk in the Alps and a close look at burrs stuck to a dog.
NASA's use of it aboard spacecraft turned it into a household name.
Its genericised trademark is a blend of the French words for velvet and hook.
puzzles.fact: George de Mestral patented it in 1955 after examining under a microscope the burdock burrs that clung to his dog on an alpine walk — an early and much-cited case of biomimicry.

hints: A handheld object of coloured squares that defined a decade of frustration.
Twenty-six smaller pieces rotate around a fixed central spindle.
It has roughly 43 quintillion reachable states, and exactly one of them is solved.
Any scramble can be undone in twenty moves or fewer, a result proven in 2010.
A Hungarian professor of architecture built it to teach students about three-dimensional form.
puzzles.fact: Its inventor built it as a teaching aid and took a month to solve his own creation. The maximum number of moves needed from any position — twenty — was proven by computer search in 2010.

hints: A brass instrument with a graduated arc, a small telescope and two mirrors.
It measures the angle between a celestial body and the horizon.
Double reflection means a slightly unsteady hand does not ruin the reading.
With an accurate clock and printed tables, that one angle yields a position line.
The graduated arc spans one sixth of a circle, which is where its name comes from.
puzzles.fact: Because it measures the angle between two things seen at once, it works from a pitching deck — the reason it replaced instruments that needed a fixed reference.

hints: A dial on the hallway wall that people tap out of pure habit.
It reads the weight of the whole atmosphere standing above you.
The aneroid kind uses a sealed metal capsule that flexes as the pressure changes.
Torricelli's original was a column of mercury standing in an open dish.
A falling reading means unsettled weather is on the way.
puzzles.fact: Tapping it is not superstition: friction can leave the needle stuck behind the true reading, and the tap frees it — which is where the phrase about tapping for an answer comes from.

hints: A glass envelope on a screw or bayonet base.
The original kind ran a tungsten thread hot enough to glow, wasting most of its energy as heat.
The gas sealed inside is inert, to stop that thread burning away.
It is the standard cartoon shorthand for suddenly having an idea.
One in a Californian fire station has reportedly been burning since 1901.
puzzles.fact: The Centennial Bulb in Livermore, California has burned almost continuously since 1901. Running well below its rated power is most of the reason it survived.

hints: A lidded vessel with a spout and a handle, central to British domestic life.
Electric versions sit on a contact base and switch themselves off unattended.
That cut-off is a bimetallic strip bent by steam travelling back down a hidden channel.
A surge in national electricity demand at the end of a popular broadcast is named after it.
The stovetop kind announces itself with a whistle instead.
puzzles.fact: British grid operators plan for "TV pickup" — a demand surge of over a gigawatt in the minutes after a big broadcast ends, as millions switch one on at once.
